I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so at the start of the year I would keep to the system I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That fits my land, the local climate, and the way I manage risk. Wheat gives me a stable first harvest, and maize after wheat makes full use of the warm rainy season. I would not spread myself across too many crops, because with my experience and schooling I prefer a simple plan I know how to manage well rather than something complicated and risky.

For seed, I would use improved or hybrid seed because I care more about stable yield and resistance than saving a little on seed. For wheat, I would use a rotary tillage system after the last maize season so I can prepare a decent seedbed without spending too much. I would apply nitrogen the most because both wheat and maize respond to it strongly, while keeping phosphorus and potassium at moderate levels so the crop does not look good early and then fall short later. Water matters a lot here, especially for wheat, because spring can be dry, so I would plan several irrigations on wheat and fewer on maize, relying partly on summer rain. I would spray pesticides only as needed but I would still expect a few applications for weeds, aphids, and common diseases, because losing control early usually costs more than spraying once or twice on time. I would keep expected yields at realistic levels, aiming for steady production rather than chasing an unusually high number.
